chunks: What an operating system is. The question: What is an operating system?
An operating system (OS) is the software layer between your programs and the hardware.
It decides which program gets the CPU and when, hands out memory, and hides hardware details behind simple calls such as "open a file". On a PC that means Windows or Linux.
On a microcontroller it is often a tiny real-time OS that does little more than switch between tasks.
Picture a restaurant kitchen with one stove and several cooks. A head chef decides who uses the stove and for how long, so every dish gets cooked and nobody waits forever.
The cooks are the programs, the stove is the CPU, and the head chef is the OS. The head chef also takes some time away from cooking, just as the OS costs some memory and CPU time.
The layering. Applications never touch the hardware directly; they call the OS, which multiplexes the resources and calls drivers.
In bare-metal firmware the top three boxes collapse into one program.
Kernel: the core of the OS that manages the CPU, memory and devices. Task: one activity the OS runs, with its own stack of working memory.
Scheduler: the part of the OS that decides which task runs next. Driver: code that hides how a particular piece of hardware works.
RTOS: ("What a real-time operating system is"): a real-time OS, a small OS that guarantees how quickly it responds.
A thermostat has three jobs. It reads a sensor every 100 milliseconds, updates the display every 500 milliseconds, and checks the buttons.
With no OS, you write one loop and do all the timing by hand. With a small OS, each job becomes its own task.
The scheduler switches between them, using the system timer, so each one can be written separately.
The cost is a little CPU time and extra RAM, because each task needs its own stack. That is the whole idea.
"An operating system is the software layer that manages hardware resources and gives applications a clean interface to them.
It handles scheduling of tasks, memory management, device drivers and I/O, and synchronisation between tasks.
On a PC that's Windows or Linux; on a microcontroller it's typically a small RTOS like FreeRTOS with a scheduler and queues.
It costs memory and CPU overhead, but makes concurrent, modular software much easier."
